# Turn a photo of your fridge into two simple dinner ideas with Meta AI

> **In short:** Meta AI can look at a photo of your fridge and suggest dinner recipes based on what it sees. Snap a wide picture, attach it to a Meta AI chat, and ask for two simple recipes — it usually returns ingredient lists, steps, and any items you'd need to buy.

Open the fridge, see half an onion, some eggs, and a slightly suspicious block of cheese, and have no idea what to cook. Sound familiar? This guide walks you through sending one photo of your fridge to Meta AI and getting two dinner ideas back, plus a quick shopping list for whatever you're missing. It's written for anyone who has never used Meta AI before — no special cooking or tech skills needed.

## Before you start

- A free Meta account. Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, or Messenger all work.
- A smartphone with one of those apps installed, **or** a browser open to the official Meta AI page.
- Roughly 5–10 minutes, including taking the photo.
- Meta AI isn't available in every country, and a few features may differ by region — if you can't find it in one app, try another.
- One honest note up front: Meta AI can read the photo and suggest ideas, but it can't actually cook, and it sometimes misreads labels or skips an item. Treat its recipes as a starting point, not a final answer.

## Step 1 — Open Meta AI in an app you already use

Pick the Meta app you use most — Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, or Messenger — and tap to open it. Once you're on the main screen, look around for a Meta AI entry point. It might look like a colorful circle icon, a search bar with "Ask Meta AI" written inside it, or a chat-style option near your other conversations. Tap whichever one you spot.

**If it looks different on your device:** Meta AI is being added to these apps in stages, so the exact placement changes often. If you don't see it inside the app, open your browser and go to the official Meta AI page instead — the experience is similar.

**You'll know it worked when** a chat screen opens with a place to type a message, usually along the bottom of the screen.

## Step 2 — Take one clear photo of your fridge

Stand in front of your open fridge with your phone's camera app open. Take a single wide photo that tries to capture as many items as possible — shelves, drawers, the door. Don't worry about neatness; Meta AI just needs to see what's there. Try to avoid bright lights behind you that would darken the fridge, and hold the phone steady for a second so the picture isn't blurry.

**If it looks different on your device:** Some phone cameras have a "wide" or "0.5x" option. Use it if you can — fitting more into one shot means fewer ingredients get missed.

**You'll know it worked when** you can clearly read labels and recognize each item when you look at the photo later.

💬 Example: a quick self-check — ask yourself, "Could a friend tell what each thing is from this picture alone?"

## Step 3 — Attach the photo and ask for two simple recipes

In the Meta AI chat, look for an attachment icon — usually a paperclip, a "+" symbol, or a small picture icon near the message box. Tap it, pick your fridge photo from the gallery, and wait a moment for the image to upload. Then type your request in plain language. Be specific: how many recipes you want, how much time you have, and any food you want to avoid.

**If it looks different on your device:** On some apps you can take the photo directly inside the chat using a camera icon, instead of choosing one from your gallery. Either way works.

**You'll know it worked when** the photo appears as a small preview in the chat, and Meta AI starts typing a reply.

💬 Example: "Here's what's in my fridge. Please suggest two simple dinner recipes I can make tonight in under 30 minutes. I don't eat pork."

## Step 4 — Refine the suggestions to fit your evening

Read through what Meta AI sent back. Often the first response is close but not quite right — maybe it suggests something spicy when you don't want spice, or a recipe that takes an hour when you only have 20 minutes. Just reply in the same chat with one short follow-up explaining what to change. Meta AI will adjust the plan.

**If it looks different on your device:** If the response stops mid-sentence or seems cut off, just send "Please continue" and it usually picks up where it left off.

**You'll know it worked when** the updated recipe matches what you actually have time, taste, and ingredients for.

💬 Example: "I don't have an oven. Can you give me a stovetop version of the second recipe?"

## Step 5 — Ask for a short shopping list of what's missing

Once you've picked a recipe you like, type one more short message asking what you'd need to buy. Meta AI compares the recipe against what it spotted in your photo and gives you a list. Ask it to keep the list short and grouped by aisle if you can — it makes the actual shopping trip faster.

**If it looks different on your device:** If Meta AI says it can't tell what's missing, just paste the recipe ingredients yourself and ask, "Which of these aren't in my fridge?" — that's usually enough to get a clean list.

**You'll know it worked when** you have a small, specific list of items to buy, not a vague "various ingredients" answer.

💬 Example: "Please make me a short shopping list of everything I'm missing from these recipes. Group it by store section."

## Step 6 — Save the recipes so you can find them while cooking

Once you're happy with the recipes and the shopping list, save them somewhere easy to reach with messy hands. On most phones you can take a screenshot of the chat, copy the recipe text into a notes app, or send it to yourself in a messaging app. The goal is to have it open on the counter without having to log in or scroll through a long chat history.

**If it looks different on your device:** If screenshots feel clunky, ask Meta AI in one final message to "summarize these recipes and the shopping list in a short format I can paste into Notes" — it usually gives you a clean block of text you can copy with one tap.

**You'll know it worked when** you can pull up the recipe and shopping list in under five seconds, even with flour on your fingers.

## Common mistakes

- **Blurry, dark photo.** The single biggest reason Meta AI gets the recipes wrong is a hard-to-read photo. Open the fridge, turn on a kitchen light, and hold still for one second before tapping the shutter. If you can't read a label in the picture, Meta AI probably can't either.
- **Asking for too much at once.** "Give me five gourmet dinners with dessert and wine pairings" overwhelms the assistant. Stick to two recipes at a time, and ask for wine or dessert in a separate follow-up if you really want it.
- **Forgetting to mention what you don't eat.** Meta AI doesn't know you're vegetarian, allergic to nuts, or out of soy sauce. The first message is the place to say so — adding it later means re-asking and getting a slightly different recipe each time.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** it's a fast way to break the "I have nothing to cook" feeling on busy weeknights. Instead of staring at the fridge for ten minutes, you spend thirty seconds taking a photo and another minute reading recipes — the rest of the time goes back to your evening.
- **For your business or work:** if you run a small café, a meal-prep service, or write a food newsletter, this is a quick brainstorming partner for "what can I make with what's on hand right now?" It won't replace a recipe developer, but it can get you past a blank page fast.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is the very next time you're stuck on dinner — open Meta AI, snap the photo, and ask for two recipes. You don't need to learn anything else first.

## Try it now

Open your fridge right now. Before you close the door, take one wide photo and send it to Meta AI with the prompt: *"Suggest two simple dinners I can make tonight in under 30 minutes with what's in this photo."* Read the first reply before you do anything else — that's the whole skill, and you already have it.
